q: In spite of wide differences in chemical properties, all the gases more or less obey the ____ laws.
e: In spite of wide differences in chemical properties, all the gases more or less obey the gas laws. The gas laws still describe pressure, volume and temperature even when the gases differ chemically.

q: The gas laws deal with how gases behave with respect to pressure, volume, temperature and ____.
e: The gas laws deal with how gases behave with respect to pressure, volume, temperature and amount. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: Boyle's law can be stated as: When the temperature of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the volume of the gas is ____ proportional to its pressure.
e: Boyle's law can be stated as: When the temperature of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the volume of the gas is inversely proportional to its pressure. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Boyle's law keeps temperature and amount fixed, so pressure and volume move in opposite directions.

q: In the 17th century, Robert Boyle, an Irish scientist, studied the behaviour of gases systematically and ____.
e: In the 17th century, Robert Boyle, an Irish scientist, studied the behaviour of gases systematically and quantitatively. Boyle's law keeps temperature and amount fixed, so pressure and volume move in opposite directions. Gas behaviour and gas reactions both matter because so much chemistry happens in the gas phase.

q: Charles' law can be stated as: When the pressure of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the volume of the gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the ____ scale.
e: Charles' law can be stated as: When the pressure of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the volume of the gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the Kelvin scale. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Gay-Lussac's pressure-temperature law says pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature at constant volume. q: In the 18th century, the French physicist ____ studied the effect of temperature on the volume of a gas at constant pressure.
e: In the 18th century, the French physicist Jacques Charles studied the effect of temperature on the volume of a gas at constant pressure. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Charles's law keeps pressure and amount fixed, so volume rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: Absolute zero temperature: The volume of a given mass of gas decreases regularly with a regular decrease in ____.
e: Absolute zero temperature: The volume of a given mass of gas decreases regularly with a regular decrease in temperature. Absolute zero is 0 K, the point where gas volume in Charles's law would theoretically hit zero.

q: If the constant contraction rate is continued, the volume of the gas will become zero at ____ $^{\circ} C$.
e: If the constant contraction rate is continued, the volume of the gas will become zero at -273 ^ degrees C. The volume of the gas will become zero at -273 ^ degrees C.

q: This temperature is taken as the zero point of a new scale of temperature(Kelvin temperature scale), and is also known as ____ zero temperature.
e: This temperature is taken as the zero point of a new scale of temperature(Kelvin temperature scale), and is also known as absolute zero temperature. Gas laws use Kelvin because that scale starts at absolute zero, where particle motion would stop. Absolute zero is 0 K, the point where gas volume in Charles's law would theoretically hit zero.

q: Gay-Lussac's law can be stated as: When a ____ of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the pressure of the gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the Kelvin scale.
e: Gay-Lussac's law can be stated as: When a volume of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the pressure of the gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the Kelvin scale. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Gay-Lussac's pressure-temperature law says pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature at constant volume. Gay-Lussac's law keeps volume and amount fixed, so pressure rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: Early in the 19th century, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, a French scientist, determined that the pressure of a gas sample increases when heated and decreases when ____ at constant volume.
e: Early in the 19th century, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, a French scientist, determined that the pressure of a gas sample increases when heated and decreases when cooled at constant volume. Gay-Lussac's law keeps volume and amount fixed, so pressure rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: STP in chemistry is the abbreviation for Standard Temperature and ____.
e: STP in chemistry is the abbreviation for Standard Temperature and Pressure. At STP you compare gases at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atm, where one mole occupies 22.4 L. Standard temperature and pressure let you compare gas amounts using a shared 22.4 L molar volume.

e: STP is commonly used when calculating gas density and volume of gas. Gas density is low because a small mass is spread through a large volume of empty space. At STP you compare gases at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atm, where one mole occupies 22.4 L.

q: There is a single expression, called the Combined Gas Law that combines Boyle's Law, Charles' Law and ____ Law.
e: There is a single expression, called the Combined Gas Law that combines Boyle's Law, Charles' Law and Gay-Lussac's Law. Boyle's law keeps temperature and amount fixed, so pressure and volume move in opposite directions. Charles's law keeps pressure and amount fixed, so volume rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: Gay-Lussac studied the volume relationship of reacting gases, and summarised the results known as Gay-Lussac's law of combining ____ of gases.

q: At the same temperature and pressure, the volumes of reacting gases and gaseous products are in simple ratios of small ____ numbers.
e: At the same temperature and pressure, the volumes of reacting gases and gaseous products are in simple ratios of small whole numbers. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: The Italian scientist ____ expressed that the volume of any given gas must be proportional to the number of moles or molecules present.
e: The Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro expressed that the volume of any given gas must be proportional to the number of moles or molecules present. Avogadro's law says equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules. Avogadro's number is about 6.02 x 10^23 particles in one mole. Avogadro links gas volume at the same T and P to the number of particles, and one mole holds 6.02 x 10^23 of them.

q: At constant temperature and pressure, the volume, V, occupied by a gas sample is directly proportional to the number of ____, n, of gas.
